Corruption Claims: Tahrif — In Both Directions

This is the core battleground. The Islamic charge is that the Bible was corrupted (tahrif). The symmetry principle (Methodology §3) requires that the same charge be tested against the Qur'an.

Part A — The Islamic doctrine of tahrif

The Qur'anic data is double-edged

Verses cited for corruption:

  • Q 2:75 — some "heard the word of Allah then distorted it knowingly."
  • Q 2:79 — "woe to those who write the book with their own hands then say 'this is from Allah'."
  • Q 3:78 — "a party twist their tongues with the Book."
  • Q 4:46, Q 5:13, Q 5:41 — "they distort words from their places."

Verses that affirm the prior scriptures in Muhammad's own time:

  • Q 5:43 — "how do they make you a judge while they have the Torah, in which is the judgment of Allah?"
  • Q 5:47 — "let the people of the Gospel judge by what Allah revealed therein."
  • Q 5:68 — "you stand on nothing until you observe the Torah and the Gospel."
  • Q 10:94 — "ask those who read the Scripture before you."
  • Q 3:3, Q 2:136 — the Torah and Gospel are confirmed.

The Qur'an itself, read internally, pushes more naturally toward tahrif al-maʿna (distortion of meaning / concealment / misreading by some) than toward tahrif al-nass (the physical text was rewritten) — otherwise commanding people to judge by the Torah/Gospel in the 7th c. would be incoherent.

The classical Muslim scholars were divided

  • Tahrif al-maʿna camp (the older, arguably majority classical view): many early exegetes, and notably al-Razi, al-Ghazali's general tendency, and others held the corruption was interpretive / concealment, the text largely standing.
  • Tahrif al-nass camp: Ibn Hazm (11th c.) argued aggressively for textual corruption of the Bible, cataloguing alleged contradictions — this became the dominant popular position later.
  • Ibn Khaldun and others noted the People of the Book still possessed their scriptures.

Modern popular apologetics vs. scholarship

  • *Ahmed Deedat, Zakir Naik, and the popular daʿwa circuit argue textual* corruption, leaning heavily on Bart Ehrman and on the Comma Johanneum, Mark 16, John 7:53–8:11, etc.
  • Scholarly assessment: the cited variants are real but limited (see Bible Transmission). They show imperfect copying, not the wholesale invention or rewriting of the Bible. Using Ehrman to prove "the Bible is fabricated" overreads him — Ehrman explicitly denies that the variants overturn the core message, and he is equally a critic of traditional Qur'anic origins claims.

Part B — The charge run in reverse (symmetry)

If textual variation, redaction, and human transmission count as "corruption" for the Bible, the same test applied to the Qur'an yields:

  • Destruction of rival codices under ʿUthman: variant readings (Ibn Masʿud's, Ubayy's) were physically eliminated. By the strict standard, suppressing variants is not the same as never having had them.
  • The Sanaa palimpsest lower text: a physical manuscript proving a different early recension existed — internal, material counter- evidence to "zero variation."
  • *The qiraʾat:* the canonical readings differ (Ḥafṣ vs. Warsh, etc.); the tradition is multiple, not singular.
  • Compositional questions: academic Qur'anic studies (Neuwirth, Sinai, Reynolds) raise editing/arrangement questions for the Qur'an just as OT scholarship does for the Pentateuch.

The point is not "therefore the Qur'an is corrupt." It is that the standard used to convict the Bible, applied evenly, also bites the Qur'an — and "an argument that proves too much fails" (Methodology §4).

Arbiter verdict — tahrif

Present.

  • Muslim case: the Qur'an accuses some People of the Book of distortion; the Bible demonstrably has variants and disputed passages; therefore the Bible is unreliable as preserved revelation.
  • Christian / academic reply: the Qur'an's own affirmation verses and the older tahrif al-maʿna reading undercut the strong textual charge; the Bible's variants are bounded and transparent; and the same skepticism applied evenly damages the Qur'an's "no variants" claim.

Weigh.

  • Strong: the Bible is not letter-perfect and was humanly transmitted/edited — true, and conceded by Christian scholarship.
  • Weak: "the Bible was wholesale rewritten/fabricated" — unsupported by manuscript evidence and not the Qur'an's own most natural claim.
  • Strong (reverse): by an even standard, the Qur'an also shows early variation (Sanaa) and a multiple reading tradition (qiraʾat); the "perfectly preserved, zero variants" claim is overstated.
  • Contested: the precise classical Muslim consensus on nass vs. maʿna — genuinely divided across history.

Judge.

  • On interpretive distortion / human transmission of the Bible: the charge is partially valid — the Bible is a humanly transmitted, variant-bearing, partly composite text. Christianity largely concedes this and reframes "preservation" as recoverability, not letter- perfection.
  • On wholesale textual fabrication of the Bible: the charge fails on the manuscript evidence and arguably fails on the Qur'an's own terms.
  • On the symmetry test: the strong-form corruption argument, applied honestly, wounds both scriptures' "perfect preservation" claims roughly equally, while leaving both core messages historically recoverable. The decisive arbiter finding here is therefore: the tahrif debate is usually won rhetorically by whoever is allowed to apply an asymmetric standard — and neither side is entitled to that.
